title: IELTS Academic Mock Test 01 — The Testly Practice Paper

parts.title: READING PASSAGE 1
passage: Urban trees are often treated as decoration, but researchers increasingly regard them as essential infrastructure. A mature tree can cool nearby streets, intercept rainwater, reduce wind and provide habitat for insects and birds. These effects are especially valuable in dense neighbourhoods where concrete and asphalt store heat during the day and release it slowly at night.

The cooling effect comes from two processes. A canopy blocks some sunlight before it reaches the ground, while the leaves release water vapour through tiny openings. This second process, called transpiration, uses heat from the surrounding air. However, trees do not all provide the same benefit. Species with broad canopies may offer more shade, whereas drought-tolerant species may survive better in warmer, drier cities.

Planning a successful urban forest therefore involves more than planting as many trees as possible. City authorities must consider soil volume, underground pipes, overhead cables and the future width of each species. Young trees are relatively cheap to plant, but they need several years of watering and protection before they become resilient. In some cities, maintenance has been neglected, leading to high mortality among newly planted trees.

Community involvement can improve the results. Residents who help choose locations or water young trees are more likely to notice disease and report damage. Some programmes also train volunteers to record flowering dates, bird sightings and canopy growth. These observations supplement professional surveys and show how urban nature changes over time.

The strongest programmes combine scientific planning with local knowledge. They place trees where shade and storm-water management are most needed, select varieties suited to the soil and climate, and budget for long-term care. The aim is not simply to make streets greener, but to create a living system that continues to serve the people who use the city.

parts.title: READING PASSAGE 2
passage: For much of history, maps were produced by specialists working with limited information. Surveyors measured distances, astronomers calculated positions and cartographers turned observations into symbols. The resulting maps could be remarkably accurate, but they were expensive and slow to update. A newly built road or a changed coastline might remain absent for years.

The arrival of aerial photography changed this process. Cameras mounted on aircraft could record large areas quickly, and overlapping photographs allowed specialists to estimate height and shape. Later, satellites extended coverage to remote regions. Yet images alone did not solve every problem: clouds could hide the ground, and the meaning of an object still required interpretation.

Digital mapping introduced another shift. Geographic information systems, or GIS, store location as data that can be combined with other datasets. A transport department can compare road accidents with lighting, speed limits and traffic volume. A conservation agency can overlay habitat, rainfall and land ownership. The map becomes a tool for asking questions rather than a fixed picture of the world.

The public now contributes to many maps. Smartphone positions, traffic reports and photographs can reveal changes almost immediately. Open mapping projects invite volunteers to trace buildings and roads from satellite imagery, which is particularly useful after earthquakes or floods. The quality of these contributions varies, so platforms use review systems and compare edits with reliable sources.

More data does not automatically produce better decisions. A map may appear precise while hiding uncertainty, outdated measurements or gaps in coverage. Designers must explain what a symbol means, when data was collected and who may be missing from it. Responsible mapping is therefore both a technical activity and an exercise in communication.

parts.title: READING PASSAGE 3
passage: Sleep is often described as a period of inactivity, but the sleeping brain is highly organised. Across a night, people move through repeating stages that differ in brain activity, muscle tone and eye movement. The exact pattern changes with age, health and recent experience, yet the sequence is not random.

One reason sleep matters is that it supports memory. During the day, new information is encoded in networks that remain vulnerable to interference. Later, during sleep, some memories are reactivated and gradually integrated with older knowledge. This process does not preserve every detail. Instead, it appears to strengthen useful patterns and may explain why people sometimes remember the general solution to a problem after sleeping.

Researchers debate how much this process depends on a particular sleep stage. Experiments that wake participants at different points have produced different results, partly because waking someone is itself disruptive. There is evidence that slow-wave sleep benefits factual learning, while periods associated with vivid dreaming may help with emotional memories and creative connections. These categories overlap, and no single stage should be treated as the brain's only learning period.

Sleep also changes the body's ability to regulate emotion. A tired person may react more strongly to an unpleasant image or interpret an ambiguous event negatively. After adequate sleep, the same person may assess the event more proportionately. This does not mean sleep removes difficult emotions; rather, it may restore the mental resources needed to place them in context.

Modern life makes regular sleep difficult. Artificial light, irregular work schedules and the expectation of constant availability can all delay bedtime. Advice that focuses only on individual discipline misses these environmental pressures. Schools, employers and designers of digital products can also influence whether people have a realistic opportunity to sleep.
